items.title: Artificial Intelligence Causal Inference of Community Clinic Postpartum Haemorrhage Risk Under Unmeasured Misoprostol Tablet Quality Degradation: A Healthcare Instrumental Variable Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Community clinic protocols for postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) prophylaxis rely on misoprostol tablets whose active-ingredient content is unobserved at the point of care, so that the protective effect of the drug is confounded by an unmeasured quality gradient that varies across batches, districts and procurement cycles. The design was evaluated by replication across 2000 cells per configuration, with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64; the analysis reports the power surface, the minimum detectable effect at 80% power, and the sampling distribution of the interaction estimator. At an intraclass correlation of 0.64, 56 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. The contribution is a design-level safety evaluation: it specifies the identification assumptions under which a quality-degradation effect is recoverable, derives the bias that arises when the exclusion restriction fails, and states the cluster counts at which a community-clinic safety study would be adequately powered. The framework is proposed, not executed on patient data; its results are design operating characteristics, not empirical estimates of misoprostol effectiveness.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Causal Inference of Community Health Worker Diagnostic Decision Support Under Unmeasured Confounding by Village-Level Supply Stockouts: A Doubly Robust Healthcare Robustness Evaluation
items.abstract: Village-level supply stockouts confound the evaluation of community health worker (CHW) diagnostic decision support because stockouts affect both the probability of algorithm-assisted diagnosis and the probability of correct treatment, and they are rarely recorded in routine data. the present analysis characterises the operating characteristics of a doubly robust before-after-control-impact (BACIP) design for estimating the effect of CHW decision support when village-level stockouts remain unmeasured. No observational data are used or claimed; the analysis is a replication-based design evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.640. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 56 clusters, and the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as clusters increase from 8 to 32. The doubly robust estimator retains nominal coverage under unmeasured village-level confounding when the treatment model includes a village stockout proxy, but coverage degrades when that proxy is omitted. The contribution is a formal statement of the conditions under which BACIP with a doubly robust estimator identifies the CHW decision-support effect, together with the cluster counts required to detect policy-relevant effects. The results imply that evaluations of CHW diagnostic support in low-resource settings should budget for at least 56 clusters and should record a village stockout indicator even when it is imperfect.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Causal Mediation Analysis of Community Health Worker Visit Frequency Effects on Childhood Immunisation Completion Under Variable Village Health Register Attrition: A Healthcare Equity Evaluation
items.abstract: Village health registers in low- and middle-income settings are the operational backbone of community health worker (CHW) programmes, yet their completeness varies systematically across villages in ways that are correlated with the very outcomes the registers are used to measure. The framework combines a potential-outcomes mediation decomposition with a bias-corrected estimating equation that treats register attrition as a village-level post-treatment confounder, and it is operationalised through a machine-learning nuisance-estimation architecture that permits flexible modelling of the visit-frequency, attrition and immunisation surfaces without imposing linearity. Because no observational data are available for the present analysis, the paper is methodological: it characterises the operating characteristics of the proposed estimator under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) using a before-after-control-impact design with 2000 replications per cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The contribution is a discipline-specific mediation framework that treats register attrition as a structural feature of CHW programme evaluation rather than as a nuisance to be discarded, and that makes the equity consequences of attrition explicit in the estimand.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Causal Transportability of Community Health Worker Triage Decision Support Under Variable Supervision Record Granularity: A Doubly Robust Evaluation of Healthcare Escalation Safety
items.abstract: Community health worker (CHW) triage decision support is increasingly proposed as a means of extending safe healthcare escalation into underserved districts, yet the safety of such systems is typically evaluated in pilot settings whose supervision records are more complete than those available at scale. the present analysis treats the resulting inferential problem as one of causal transportability under a before-after-control-impact (BACI) design and characterises the operating characteristics of a doubly robust estimator when supervision record granularity varies. No observational data are used or claimed; the analysis is a design-based evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty clusters were required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power. The paper derives the transportability conditions under which a doubly robust BACI contrast identifies the escalation-safety effect, shows how record granularity enters as a coarsening of the supervision covariate, and specifies the design quantities that a field evaluation must report. The contribution is a formal account of when CHW triage decision support can be expected to transport across supervision regimes, together with the sample-size consequences of that account.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Computer Vision for Sickle Cell Retinopathy Screening Under Variable Fundus Camera Flash Intensity: A Test-Time Calibration Evaluation of Healthcare Referral Sensitivity
items.abstract: Sickle cell retinopathy screening programmes that deploy artificial intelligence (AI) computer vision on fundus photographs face a calibration problem that is rarely modelled explicitly: flash intensity varies across cameras, operators and clinic conditions, and a classifier trained at one illumination level may shift its referral threshold when deployed at another. the present analysis treats test-time calibration as a design problem for referral sensitivity rather than as a post-hoc correction. It formalises flash-induced intensity shift as a monotone transform of the retinal image, derives the conditions under which a temperature-scaling calibrator fitted on source-illumination data preserves the referral decision boundary at target illumination, and characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact (BACI) evaluation of calibration transfer. The design uses 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64.56 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point referral-sensitivity gain at 80% power, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 dominates the detectable effect more than the calibration method itself. The contribution is a formal account of when test-time calibration can be trusted to preserve referral sensitivity, and a design-level statement of the cluster counts that screening programmes must budget for if they intend to evaluate calibration transfer empirically.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Conformalised Counterfactual Policy Learning for Community Clinic Referral Escalation Under Unobserved Acuity Drift: A Healthcare Regret-Bound Evaluation
items.abstract: Community clinic referral escalation policies must decide which patients to send onward when patient acuity is only partially observed and drifts over time. The framework treats unobserved acuity drift as a bounded distribution shift and constructs conformal prediction regions that remain valid under that shift, then uses these regions to define a pessimistic policy class whose worst-case regret can be bounded in closed form. The analysis yields three results: a drift-robust conformal guarantee, a regret decomposition separating approximation error from conformal coverage slack, and a finite-sample bound that scales with the square root of the drift budget. The paper also reports a real-data calibration exercise using World Bank World Development Indicators for 24 African countries over 2000-2023 (N = 560), estimated by OLS with heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 standard errors, yielding R-squared = 0.591, adjusted R-squared = 0.5895, F = 184.764 (p = 2.82e-62), with coefficients for access to electricity (1291.55405, SE 194.35159), urban population (113.13952, SE 7.77493) and a linear year term (-104.41834, SE 11.31314). This exercise illustrates the magnitude of drift that a referral policy must tolerate. The contribution is a formal bridge between conformal inference and counterfactual policy learning for referral escalation, with explicit regret bounds that make the cost of unobserved acuity drift auditable.

items.abstract: Electrocardiograph lead reversal is a common, frequently undetected pre-analytical error in community clinic chest pain triage, and its interaction with artificial-intelligence-based decision support has not been characterised as a safety-guarantee problem. The framework treats lead reversal as a latent nuisance parameter that perturbs the feature distribution, and it constructs triage sets whose coverage guarantee is conditional on a declared exchangeability assumption that reversal violates. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5-percentage-point effect. The contribution is a formal statement of the conditions under which conformal triage guarantees survive lead reversal, together with the design parameters that a safety evaluation must satisfy to detect guarantee failure.

The problem is solved by an artificial-intelligence search procedure that combines a constrained Pareto local search with a surrogate model of adherence response. Because no field data are available, the evaluation is a replication study: a before-after-control-impact design is characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, and power is estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80% power at 52 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect. Reconciliation error acts as a constraint on achievable equity rather than as noise to be averaged away, and that the optimiser's equity penalty must be set from the design's minimum detectable effect rather than from the observed adherence gap. The contribution is a formalisation that makes the equity cost of stock-record error explicit and a design rule that ties optimisation targets to the power of the evaluation that will judge them.

items.abstract: Antivenom stockouts in low-resource health systems are driven less by average demand than by the interaction between stochastic power outages and the cold-chain constraints that make replenishment irreversible once a vial is compromised. the present analysis formulates antivenom replenishment as a constrained Markov decision process in which the decision-maker observes refrigerator state, outage duration, and stock on hand, and chooses order quantities subject to a cold-chain loss probability that depends on outage length. A constrained reinforcement learning procedure is proposed that maximises expected service level subject to an explicit budget on expected wastage, using a Lagrangian relaxation whose multiplier is adapted online. Because no field data are available, the design is evaluated through a replication-based replication study that characterises the operating characteristics of the before-after-control-impact estimator used to assess the intervention. The replication uses a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5, and an intraclass correlation of 0.64, with 2000 replications per design cell across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power under this variance structure. The contribution is a formalisation of cold-chain-constrained replenishment as a safe reinforcement learning problem together with a design-analysis protocol that specifies the cluster counts at which such an intervention could be credibly evaluated.

The contribution is a transportability bound that separates gain-drift magnitude from calibration error and shows that counterfactual recalibration is identifiable only when the drift is monotone and the anchor set is gain-invariant. The framework separates the causal estimand from the logging mechanism, permits sensitivity analysis to logging error, and yields a defensible basis for workload-equity claims when competency records are imperfect.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Doubly Robust Estimation of Community Health Worker Triage Accuracy Under Differential Verification by Referral Distance: A Healthcare Selection-Bias Evaluation
items.abstract: Community health worker (CHW) triage programmes routinely verify only a subset of referrals, and verification is often more likely for patients living near a referral facility. This differential verification by referral distance creates a selection bias that inflates naive estimates of triage accuracy. Because no field data are available, the estimator's finite-sample behaviour is characterised in a replication study of 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2). Across the replications the estimated bias was 0.04454 for the intercept and -0.00104 for the exposure coefficient; the root mean squared error was 0.91714 and 0.01621 respectively; and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The results indicate that the doubly robust estimator is approximately unbiased for the exposure coefficient and that its confidence intervals attain nominal coverage under the stated process, while the intercept exhibits small positive bias. Differential verification by referral distance is a structural feature of CHW programmes rather than a nuisance, and that doubly robust estimation should be the default analytic strategy for triage-accuracy evaluations.

items.abstract: Paper electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings remain the dominant medium for cardiac triage in many African healthcare settings, yet chart recorder speed calibration varies across devices and over time, systematically distorting the time axis on which automated interpretation depends. the present analysis formalises the problem as a domain shift in the sampling operator of a convolutional ECG classifier and proposes a calibration-aware domain adaptation framework that estimates the effective paper speed from the trace itself and resamples to a canonical 25 mm/s grid before inference. Because no observational corpus of calibrated paper ECGs was available, the framework's operating characteristics were characterised analytically and through a design-based power analysis of the before-after-control-impact estimator used to evaluate triage accuracy in a planned multi-site deployment. Under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 percentage points, residual standard deviation of 4.5 percentage points and intraclass correlation of 0.64, the analysis indicates that 56 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point improvement in triage accuracy at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. The contribution is a formalisation of speed-calibration shift as a domain adaptation problem, a resampling-based correction whose error propagation is bounded, and a design analysis that specifies the evidence required before clinical deployment claims can be made.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Free Flap Monitoring in Reconstructive Surgery: A Review
items.abstract: Free flap reconstruction is widely used in reconstructive surgery, but postoperative vascular compromise remains a major cause of flap failure. Early detection of arterial insufficiency and venous congestion is essential for timely intervention and flap salvage. Conventional monitoring is limited by observer variability, flap accessibility, and assessment frequency. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support more consistent and continuous surveillance. This review examines the diagnostic performance, clinical utility, implementation challenges, and research priorities of AI-based postoperative free flap monitoring. Applications include smartphone photography, serial clinical images, thermal imaging, near-infrared spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging, and other monitoring signals. Tasks encompass classification, segmentation, severity grading, and longitudinal prediction, distinguishing detection of existing perfusion abnormalities from prediction of subsequent compromise. Emerging studies report promising performance in identifying impaired perfusion; however, diagnostic accuracy alone does not establish clinical effectiveness. Limitations include small or single-center cohorts, image-level data leakage, class imbalance, inconsistent reference standards, limited external validation, and insufficient evidence of improved flap salvage. Performance may vary with flap location, tissue characteristics, skin pigmentation, image quality, and monitoring protocols. Intraoral and buried flaps pose additional accessibility challenges. Safe implementation requires standardized data acquisition, transparent alert thresholds, clinician oversight, privacy protection, and clear escalation pathways. AI may complement established clinical assessment, but routine adoption requires multicentre validation and prospective evidence of clinical benefit. Future studies should prioritize patient-level performance, detection time, false-negative events, unnecessary alerts, workload, flap salvage, and patient outcomes.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance of Clinical Algorithm Registries Under Unmeasured Post-Market Performance Drift Reporting: A Healthcare Political Accountability Evaluation
items.abstract: Clinical algorithm registries are increasingly proposed as the institutional mechanism through which health systems will govern artificial intelligence at the point of care, yet the political accountability they promise depends on a reporting infrastructure that does not currently exist. the present analysis develops a political-science evaluation of registry governance under conditions of unmeasured post-market performance drift, the gradual divergence between algorithm behaviour and the population it serves that occurs after deployment and that no existing registry instrument captures. The argument is that the accountability deficit is not a technical measurement problem awaiting a better sensor but a constitutional problem of delegation: registries allocate discretion to algorithm developers and to the agencies that certify them without creating a corresponding obligation to report drift, and without a reporting obligation there is no audit trail against which political principals can hold anyone to account. The paper specifies the institutional design conditions under which a drift-reporting obligation would restore accountability, distinguishes monitoring from verification, and identifies the boundary conditions under which registry-based accountability fails. The contribution is a governance-theoretic account of why post-market surveillance of clinical algorithms cannot be treated as an extension of pre-market approval, and a set of design propositions for legislatures and health agencies that wish to close the accountability gap.

items.abstract: Community health data trusts are being proposed across sub-Saharan Africa as vehicles for the secondary use of routine health information, yet the political legitimacy of the consent arrangements that would authorise them remains unmeasured wherever traditional authority exercises jurisdiction over the communities whose data are held. The framework specifies four legitimacy dimensions—authorisation, accountability, contestability and representational adequacy—and derives the conditions under which each is satisfied, strained or defeated when the boundaries of traditional authority jurisdiction are unknown. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised for the empirical evaluation of trust interventions, with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80 per cent power. Legitimacy deficits in this setting are structural rather than remediable by better consent instruments, and that AI governance for community health data trusts must incorporate jurisdictional uncertainty as a design parameter rather than as a residual risk.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance of Differential Privacy Budget Allocation in Federated Clinical Learning Under Unmeasured Health Ministry Disclosure Audit Frequency: A Healthcare Privacy-Political Bargaining Evaluation
items.abstract: Differential privacy budget allocation in federated clinical learning is typically treated as a technical parameter to be optimised against model utility. The budget is more accurately understood as a political resource whose allocation is negotiated between health ministries, clinical sites and AI developers, and that the governance of this allocation is distorted when the frequency of ministry disclosure audits is unmeasured. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator is used to characterise the operating characteristics of a design that would recover audit-frequency effects under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required for 80 per cent power at a 5 percentage point effect, and that the intraclass correlation of 0.64 substantially constrains what federated designs can detect. The paper concludes that privacy budget governance requires an explicit audit-frequency reporting regime, without which bargaining outcomes remain unverifiable and accountability is structurally deferred.

items.abstract: Emergency department triage acuity models increasingly rely on artificial intelligence to rank patients, yet their governance assumes that the main threat to fairness is measurement error in clinical variables. A more consequential threat is political: nurse union staffing grievance escalation is an unmeasured institutional signal that shapes how triage scores are produced, contested and overridden, and it is systematically absent from the data on which fairness audits depend. Because no observational data are available, the framework is operationalised as a before-after-control-impact design and its operating characteristics are characterised under a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster SD of 6.0 and residual SD of 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points; 54 clusters are required for 80% power at a 5 percentage point effect. The contribution is a governance argument that fairness evaluation must model the political production of triage data, not only its statistical properties.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance of Health Worker Strike Contingency Rostering Models Under Unmeasured Union Bargaining Exemption Clauses: A Political replication Evaluation
items.abstract: Contingency rostering models used in health workforce governance during strikes typically treat union bargaining exemptions as exogenous constraints, yet these exemptions are often unmeasured and politically negotiated. Using a replication-based design with 600 data sets of N = 500 drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2), the study characterises the ordinary least squares estimator for the parameters intercept, exposure, group and severity. The results show that the intercept was estimated with a bias of -0.06299 and an RMSE of 0.91371, while the exposure coefficient had a bias of 0.00125 and an RMSE of 0.01647; empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The sampling distribution of the exposure coefficient approximated normality, as did the Q-Q plot. A receiver operating characteristic curve was generated to assess a binary classification derived from the exposure coefficient. Unmeasured union bargaining exemption clauses introduce a structural misspecification that is not captured by conventional estimator diagnostics, and that AI governance frameworks for strike contingency rostering must incorporate political measurement of exemption clauses as a precondition for valid inference. The contribution is a methodological demonstration that political replication can expose the fragility of rostering models when key governance variables remain unmeasured.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Governance of Predictive Sepsis Alert Suppression Under Unmeasured Nurse Workload Adaptation: A Healthcare Political Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Predictive sepsis alert systems increasingly incorporate suppression logic that withholds alerts when the clinical workload of the receiving unit is judged to be high. Such suppression constitutes a political act of rationing that is rendered invisible by the absence of any measurement of nurse workload adaptation, and it evaluates the safety of suppression governance through a replication-based design analysis. The study characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and residual standard deviation of 4.5. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power, a requirement that exceeds the cluster counts typically available to hospital sepsis programmes. The paper concludes that governance of alert suppression must treat nurse workload adaptation as a measurable political variable rather than an unmeasured confounder, and it specifies the institutional conditions under which suppression can be rendered accountable.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Plastic and Hand Surgery – Potential or Provocation?
items.abstract: Introduction: Surgical specialities like plastic and hand surgery, which depend on precision, aesthetic, and functional outcomes, are integrating AI, creating potential and challenges. AI is rapidly transforming clinical procedures, requiring evaluation of its potential to improve clinical care and the challenges it faces. This narrative review critically evaluates the clinical applications, emerging innovations, and ethical challenges of AI in plastic and hand surgery, synthesising evidence on both its transformative potential and the challenges it presents.Method: We conducted a narrative review of peer-reviewed literature using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (2018-2025). Keywords included “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “plastic surgery,” “hand surgery,” “microsurgery,” and “convolutional neural networks.” We included studies on clinical applications, technological innovations, and ethical considerations. This review differs from existing syntheses by providing a balanced “Potential vs Provocation” framework that systematically addresses both benefits and challenges while proposing concrete implementation strategies for clinical practice.Results: AI technologies such as convolutional neural networks and large language models classify skin lesions, evaluate aesthetics, and automate operative documentation.Conclusion: Innovations such as generative AI, mixed reality, and predictive analytics in microsurgical procedures, patient-specific simulations, and smart rehabilitation have driven tremendous advances in this field. Despite this potential, significant challenges remain, including data bias, limited AI model interpretability, and concerns about liability and privacy. AI in plastic and hand surgery has significant potential to strengthen surgeons; however, integrating it requires acceptance, education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical guidelines to address the challenges of this technological evolution.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in Saudi otolaryngology research: a scoping review of the current landscape, gaps, and future directions
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in otolaryngology, but the extent and focus of AI research in Saudi Arabia remain unclear. This scoping review mapped the available evidence and identified key research themes and knowledge gaps. Methods A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Saudi Medical Journal archive were searched for studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Eligible studies investigated AI applications or clinician perspectives within Saudi otolaryngology. The evidence was mapped across major otolaryngology domains, including cochlear implantation and hearing, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, head and neck oncology, surgical and other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea, AI education and implementation, and AI-assisted patient education. Results The searches identified 2,925 database records, four records from other sources and seven records from an updated search and expert suggestions; thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence covered AI awareness and education, large language model (LLM)-based patient education, cochlear implantation, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, and head and neck oncology; no eligible study addressed surgical or other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinicians were generally positive about AI, while clinical studies showed promising performance of AI models. LLM chatbots generally gave accurate postoperative advice, although, when validated tools were used, their responses were harder to read and less actionable than patient-education standards recommend. However, limited AI education, small or non-Saudi datasets, limited external validation, and implementation barriers remained important challenges. Conclusion AI research in Saudi otolaryngology remains limited but is expanding across several clinical domains. Future research should prioritise Saudi-specific datasets, multicentre clinical validation, structured AI education, rigorous bilingual (Arabic and English) evaluation of LLM-generated patient information, and safe integration of AI into clinical practice in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Inference of Community Clinic Malaria Chemoprophylaxis Breakthrough Under Unmeasured Bed Net Repellent Resistance: A Healthcare Doubly Robust Effectiveness Evaluation
items.abstract: Community clinic malaria chemoprophylaxis programmes are evaluated with before-after-control-impact designs that assume bed net repellent resistance is either absent or fully measured. When resistance is unmeasured, the interaction term that identifies prophylaxis breakthrough absorbs the resistance effect, and the resulting estimator is biased in a direction that depends on the correlation between resistance and the intervention. the present analysis characterises the operating characteristics of a doubly robust before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design required 54 clusters to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 per cent power. The doubly robust estimator retains nominal coverage when the resistance model is misspecified but the treatment model is correct, and that the minimum detectable effect rises steeply below 24 clusters. The contribution is a design-level characterisation of when doubly robust inference can substitute for measured resistance, and a boundary condition: below 24 clusters the estimator's bias correction is itself too variable to be trusted.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Inference of Community Clinic Neonatal Jaundice Treatment Thresholds Under Unmeasured Transcutaneous Bilirubin Device Calibration Drift: A Healthcare Distributionally Robust Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Transcutaneous bilirubinometry is the primary screening modality for neonatal jaundice in community clinics, yet device calibration drift is unmeasured in routine practice and can silently shift measured bilirubin concentrations relative to the serum values on which treatment thresholds were established. The framework is formalised through a robust optimisation problem whose solution yields drift-adjusted treatment thresholds, and the safety guarantee is expressed as a bound on the probability of failing to treat a neonate whose true serum bilirubin exceeds the clinical action level. A design and power analysis of the before-after-control-impact estimator used to evaluate threshold revisions is reported: under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage-point change at 80% power, and power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The contribution is a formal bridge between distributionally robust optimisation and neonatal jaundice safety policy, together with an evaluation design that makes the safety consequences of threshold revision estimable before deployment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Inpatient Deterioration Forecasting Under Variable Nurse Charting Interval Irregularity: An Irregular-Time Hawkes Process Evaluation of Healthcare Rapid-Response Activation
items.abstract: Nurse charting intervals in inpatient wards are irregular, and the irregularity is informative: deteriorating patients are charted more often, so the observation times of a deterioration-forecasting model depend on the outcome the model is meant to predict. the present analysis treats that dependence as the central methodological problem for artificial-intelligence rapid-response activation and proposes an irregular-time Hawkes process in which the charting intensity and the deterioration intensity are jointly specified, with the charting process carrying a self-exciting term that responds to the patient's latent deterioration state. The proposal is evaluated as a design study rather than an empirical trial: no observational data are used or claimed, and the operating characteristics of the before-after-control-impact estimator that would be used to evaluate a deployed system are characterised under a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, a requirement that exceeds every cluster count in the evaluated grid. The forecasting problem and the evaluation problem are coupled: a model that conditions on charting irregularity changes the very activation rate that the before-after-control-impact estimator is designed to measure, and evaluation designs that ignore this coupling will misstate the effect of deployment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Mammography Screening Recall Under Variable Film Digitizer Grayscale Response: A Phantom-Reanchored Calibration Evaluation of Healthcare Diagnostic Yield
items.abstract: Film digitizers used to convert analogue mammograms into digital images vary in their grayscale response, and this variation propagates into the pixel values on which artificial intelligence (AI) screening classifiers are trained and deployed. The paper treats the resulting calibration problem as a formal measurement problem rather than a data-augmentation problem. A phantom-reanchored calibration operator is defined that maps each digitizer's grayscale response onto a common reference response using a calibration phantom, and the operating characteristics of AI recall decisions under that operator are characterised analytically. The analysis is a design and power study, not an observational one: no mammographic images or patient records were used. Under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, the before-after-control-impact estimator was evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Fifty-four clusters were required to detect a 5 percentage point recall effect at 80 per cent power. items.title: Artificial Intelligence Off-Policy Evaluation of Sequential Community Clinic Triage Decisions Under Delayed Referral Feedback: A Healthcare Counterfactual Estimator Validity Analysis
items.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) promises to estimate the value of sequential triage policies from logged community-clinic data, but referral outcomes arrive late and selectively, so the logging policy and the target policy are confounded by the same unobserved severity that drives both the decision and the eventual label. the present analysis treats the validity of counterfactual triage estimators as a formal problem rather than an empirical one. It specifies a sequential decision model in which triage actions, delayed referral feedback and latent severity interact, and it derives the conditions under which importance-sampling, self-normalised and doubly robust estimators remain consistent when feedback is delayed and missing not at random. The central result is a bias decomposition that separates the delay-induced selection term from the variance term, and a proposition showing that doubly robust estimation removes the first-order selection bias only when the propensity model is correctly specified on the observed history. A replication-based evaluation of the ['Intercept', 'exposure', 'group', 'severity'] estimator was conducted: 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2), and the study characterises the behaviour of the ordinary least squares estimator under the stated process. Across the 600 replications the estimated bias was -0.00378 for the intercept and 0.00033 for exposure, with RMSE 0.8621 and 0.015 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% intervals was 1.0 for both parameters. The analysis clarifies which OPE estimators can be trusted for sequential triage and under what identification assumptions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Referral for Retinopathy of Prematurity Under Variable Wide-Field Camera Availability: A Cascaded Calibration Evaluation of Healthcare Transfer Timing
items.abstract: Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) remains a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness, and artificial intelligence (AI) referral systems based on wide-field digital retinal imaging have been proposed to extend screening into districts where ophthalmologists are scarce. Such systems are typically evaluated on image-level discrimination, yet their clinical value depends on a cascaded decision: an image must first be acquired with a camera that is available, then classified with a calibration that transfers across device makes, and only then converted into a transfer decision whose timing is safe. The analysis treats camera availability as a latent regime that governs both the probability of acquiring a gradable image and the calibration of the AI classifier, and it derives the distribution of referral timing error as a function of regime-conditional sensitivity, specificity and acquisition probability. Using a declared variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5, the design analysis shows that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework clarifies why image-level performance metrics overstate referral safety when camera regimes are heterogeneous, and it identifies the calibration-transfer step as the dominant source of timing error under realistic availability constraints. The contribution is a design-level account of when cascaded AI referral can be trusted for ROP transfer decisions, and a specification of the evidence that a calibration-transfer evaluation must report.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence replication of Community Health Worker Diagnostic Image Triage Under Unmeasured Smartphone Camera White-Balance Drift: A Healthcare Fairness-Robustness Evaluation
items.abstract: Smartphone-based diagnostic image triage by community health workers is vulnerable to unmeasured white-balance drift, a camera-level nuisance that shifts colour distributions and can systematically distort the classifier outputs on which triage decisions depend. The framework is operationalised through a replication-based replication in which 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process with intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35 and error SD 4.2, and the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised across replications. The replication returned estimated biases of 0.00145 for the intercept and 2e-05 for the exposure coefficient, root mean squared errors of 0.84328 and 0.0153 respectively, and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence intervals of 1.0 for both parameters. These results establish a baseline against which drift-induced distortion can be quantified, and they show that under a correctly specified linear process the estimator is essentially unbiased and its intervals are conservative. Fairness-robustness evaluation of image triage must separate camera-level nuisance from label-level signal, and it proposes a decomposition that locates white-balance drift in the input distribution rather than in the decision rule.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence replication of District Hospital Computed Tomography Triage Under Unmeasured Contrast Media Viscosity Drift: A Healthcare Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) triage in district hospitals increasingly relies on automated contrast-enhanced protocols whose safety margins depend on contrast media viscosity, a property that is rarely measured at the point of care and that drifts with storage temperature and formulation variability. The framework couples a pharmacokinetic contrast-transport model to a triage classifier and derives a viscosity-drift sensitivity bound on triage error. A replication-based evaluation was conducted: 600 data sets of N = 500 were drawn from a declared data-generating process (intercept 12.0, exposure 0.42, group -3.1, severity 1.35, error SD 4.2), and the behaviour of the ordinary least squares estimator was characterised under the stated process. The estimator recovered the exposure coefficient with negligible bias (-0.00108) and empirical coverage of the nominal 95% confidence interval of 1.0 for both intercept and exposure, while the intercept bias was 0.07473 with RMSE 0.92702. The framework proposes that viscosity drift acts as a structured perturbation whose safety consequence is bounded by the classifier's margin distribution rather than by its average accuracy, and it identifies the conditions under which triage safety claims remain valid without direct viscosity measurement.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Sparse-Data Transfer Learning for Neonatal Jaundice Risk Inference Under Variable Transcutaneous Bilirubin Device Calibration: A computed Healthcare Safety Evaluation
items.abstract: Transcutaneous bilirubin (TcB) devices enable non-invasive neonatal jaundice screening, but their calibration drifts across device generations, skin phototypes and clinical sites, and sparse local data prevent site-specific recalibration. The framework combines a shared spectral representation with device-specific affine correction and a risk-calibrated decision threshold, and it is evaluated through a replication study that characterises the operating characteristics of the before-after-control-impact design under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells with 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points.50 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power, and that the minimum detectable effect at 80% power falls steeply as cluster count rises from 8 to 32. The framework proposes that calibration-aware transfer learning can reduce false-negative risk under device heterogeneity, but the design analysis indicates that sparse-data safety claims require cluster counts well above those typical of single-site evaluations. The contribution is a formalisation of calibration shift as a domain-adaptation problem and a design-level account of the evidence needed before such inference can be deployed safely.
